sections.h: Ezekiel: the Sabbath as the sign Israel profaned
sections.b: Ezekiel makes the Sabbath the test of Israel's loyalty. In his history of Israel (Ezekiel 20) the LORD gives the Sabbaths in the wilderness "as a sign between me and them", and every generation profanes them (Ezekiel 20:12–13, 16, 20–21, 24). The indictment of Jerusalem says that Jerusalem has "profaned my Sabbaths" (Ezekiel 22:8) and says the priests "have closed their eyes" to them (Ezekiel 22:26). In Ezekiel 23:38 the women profane the Sabbaths on the same day they defile the sanctuary. For exiles far from the Temple, the Sabbath was a practice they could keep anywhere.

common: Ezekiel's emphasis on the Sabbath helped make it a mark of Jewish identity in exile.
uncommon: Some scholars think the Sabbath emphasis in Ezekiel is partly the work of priestly editors in the exile.

sections.h: Ezekiel: children given to the fire
sections.b: Ezekiel never names Molech, but he speaks of children "made to pass through the fire" (Ezekiel 20:31; 16:21) and of the firstborn who "pass over" (Ezekiel 20:26). Ezekiel 23:37, 39 charges Oholah and Oholibah with killing their children for idols and then entering the Temple the same day. Ezekiel 20:25–26 alone says that the LORD gave Israel "rules that were not good" and made them unclean through the sacrifice of the firstborn, a verse that has kept readers busy since antiquity.

sections.h: Ezekiel 20:25–26: the firstborn and the "rules that were not good"
sections.b: Exodus 13:2 asks that every firstborn be set apart to the LORD, and Exodus 22:29 says, "Give me the firstborn of your sons." Ezekiel 20:26 speaks of "every opener of a womb", the Torah's own words for the firstborn, and says the LORD defiled Israel through this offering "to leave them horrified". Whether Ezekiel means that the law of the firstborn was once read as a demand for sacrifice (Levenson), or that God gave them over to the practice as a judgment, is disputed. Every reading admits that the verse is among the hardest in the Bible.

sections.h: Ezekiel's three words for the objects of idolatry
sections.b: Ezekiel uses three Hebrew words that English often runs together. Gillulim ("filthy idols") is a word of contempt used about 39 times (for example Ezekiel 20:7, 16, 18, 24, 31; 22:3–4; 23:7, 30, 37, 39). Shiqqutsim ("detestable things") are the cult objects that disgust (Ezekiel 20:7–8). To'evot ("abhorrent things") are the acts and practices that God cannot bear (Ezekiel 20:4; 22:2; 23:36). Chapter 20 charges that Israel served the idols of Egypt from the start (Ezekiel 20:7–8).

sections.h: Ezekiel 20: the exodus told as rebellion, and a new exodus
sections.b: Ezekiel 20 retells the exodus as a story of rebellion at every stage, from Egypt (20:5–9) through the wilderness (20:10–26) to the land (20:27–31), with the LORD acting "for the sake of my name" each time. Then it promises a second exodus: the LORD will bring his people out with a strong hand and an outstretched arm from the nations into the wilderness of the peoples, and will sort them before he brings them into the land (Ezekiel 20:33–38). The new exodus is a judgment as well as a rescue.

sections.h: Ezekiel 21:21: the king of Babylon's three omens
sections.b: Ezekiel 21:21 names three methods of reading omens used by the king of Babylon at the fork of two roads: shaking arrows, asking the teraphim, and examining the liver. The teraphim here are household or divinatory images, as in Genesis 31:19 and Judges 17:5; Zechariah 10:2 says they "speak nonsense". Examining a sheep's liver was a major Mesopotamian art, and clay models of livers survive. The verse is the only place where the Bible shows a foreign king using all three together.

sections.h: Ezekiel 21:27: "until he comes whose right it is"
sections.b: Ezekiel 21:27 promises that the ruin will continue "until he comes whose right it is", and "to him I will give it". The line has been tied to Genesis 49:10 ("until Shiloh comes"). Christian tradition has read it of Christ. Rashi and the Targum of Ezekiel, as read on Sefaria, apply it to figures of Ezekiel's own time (the one appointed to judge; Ishmael son of Nethaniah). Many modern commentators hear an echo of Genesis 49:10 and a promise of the rightful Davidic ruler of Ezekiel 34:23–24 and 37:24.

Ezekiel calls Jerusalem "the city of bloodshed" ('ir hadamim) at Ezekiel 22:2 and 24:6, 9. The charge covers murder, judicial killing for bribes, and idols, which are set beside blood (Ezekiel 22:3–4, 6, 9, 12). Ezekiel 24:7–8 adds that the city left its blood on a bare rock, uncovered, so that it would call for vengeance, as Abel's blood did (Genesis 4:10; Leviticus 17:13).

sections.h: Ezekiel 21–24: the sword, the furnace and the cup
sections.b: The LORD's anger in this part of Ezekiel takes four pictures: the sword drawn from its sheath (Ezekiel 21:3–5, 9–17), the furnace in which Israel is melted as dross (Ezekiel 22:17–22), the cup of horror given first to Samaria and then to Jerusalem (Ezekiel 23:31–34), and the pot on the fire (Ezekiel 24:3–14). Each picture ends with the LORD letting his rage "rest" (Ezekiel 21:17; 24:13), as though the judgment has a purpose and an end.

sections.h: Ezekiel 23–24: the Temple defiled and taken
sections.b: Ezekiel 23:38–39 says that Oholah and Oholibah defiled the sanctuary and profaned the Sabbaths on the same day they killed their children for idols, then came into the LORD's house. Ezekiel 24:21 says the LORD will "profane" the sanctuary itself, "the boast of your strength, the delight of your eyes", and ties its loss to the death of the prophet's wife. The Temple was burned in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:9).

Ezekiel 23 tells of two sisters, Oholah (Samaria) and Oholibah (Jerusalem), who are the LORD's wives and who prostitute themselves with Assyria, Egypt and Babylon. It joins Ezekiel 16, Hosea 1–3 and Jeremiah 3:6–11 as one of the Bible's marriage allegories of Israel's unfaithfulness. Modern readers divide over whether its sexual violence can be read as only a metaphor: critics such as Galambush and Weems argue that it harms; Block, Greenberg and Joyce defend it as a shocking picture of a covenant broken.

sections.h: Ezekiel 22:30: no one in the gap
sections.b: In Ezekiel 22:30 the LORD says he looked for someone "to build a wall and stand in the gap in front of me for the land", and found no one. Psalm 106:23 says Moses stood in the breach, and Jeremiah 5:1 sends the searcher through Jerusalem's streets for one honest person. The Greek of Codex Vaticanus lacks the wall and the gap. The verse is used in prayer for intercession; it also says that the judgment came after a search for help that did not succeed.

sections.h: Ezekiel 23: Samaria and Jerusalem as lovers of the empires
sections.b: Ezekiel 23 treats Israel's and Judah's alliances with Assyria, Egypt and Babylon as unfaithfulness in a marriage. Samaria turns to Assyria and is given to it (23:5–10). Jerusalem lusts for Assyria, then sends messengers to Chaldea after seeing painted pictures of its officers, and later returns to Egypt (23:11–21). The lovers then turn on her (23:22–35). The historical background includes Menahem and Hoshea (2 Kings 15; 17), Ahaz (2 Kings 16), Hezekiah (Isaiah 39) and Zedekiah (Ezekiel 17:13–15).

sections.h: Ezekiel 24:1 and the day the siege began
sections.b: Ezekiel dates his word to the tenth day of the tenth month of the ninth year of Jehoiachin's exile (Ezekiel 24:1), the day 2 Kings 25:1 and Jeremiah 52:4 give for Nebuchadnezzar's arrival at Jerusalem; Jeremiah 39:1 gives the same year and month but no day. Ezekiel counts years from the exile of 597 BC, which began Zedekiah's reign, so the ninth year of the exile is Zedekiah's ninth. By the usual count the day was in January 588 BC. Counting the years from autumn puts the fall of Jerusalem in July 586, about 30 months after that day; counting from spring puts it in July 587, about 18 months after, with the same day for the siege's start.

sections.h: Ezekiel's sign acts in chapters 21 and 24
sections.b: In this part of Ezekiel the prophet acts out the message. He groans "with your hips breaking" before the elders (Ezekiel 21:6), marks two roads on the ground for the king of Babylon (21:19), and, on the death of his wife, forbids himself all mourning (24:16–24). Two of these have a date or a day: the siege-day of Ezekiel 24:1, and the evening of his wife's death (24:18). The muteness of Ezekiel 3:26–27 ends with the survivor's arrival (24:27; 33:22).

sections.h: Ezekiel 21 and 24: the groan, the two roads and the silent mourning
sections.b: Three sign acts fall in this part of Ezekiel. In Ezekiel 21:6–7 the prophet groans with his hips breaking before the elders, so that they ask why and he can tell them of the news that is coming. In 21:19–20 he marks out two roads on the ground for the king of Babylon, one to Rabbah of Ammon and one to Jerusalem. In 24:15–24 his wife dies and he is forbidden every rite of mourning, so that the exiles will see what they will do when the Temple is taken. The third is also a sign of the muteness that ends in 24:27 and 33:22.

sections.h: Ezekiel 21:25–27: the profane and wicked leader
sections.b: Ezekiel does not name Zedekiah, but 21:25–27 is usually read of him. The "profane and wicked leader of Israel" is told to take off the turban and the crown, for nothing will stay as it was, and the ruin will last until "he comes whose right it is". Ezekiel's word for him is nasi "leader", not "king". The oath he broke to Nebuchadnezzar is the subject of Ezekiel 17:13–19, and the omen of 21:21–23 says that Jerusalem's people will take it as a false divination because they have sworn oaths.

sections.h: Ezekiel 24:1 and the first day of the siege
sections.b: Ezekiel 24:1–2 dates the beginning of the siege to the tenth day of the tenth month of the ninth year, and says that the king of Babylon "has leaned his weight against Jerusalem on this very day". Second Kings 25:1 and Jeremiah 52:4 give the same day; Jeremiah 39:1 gives the same year and month without the day. The pot of 24:3–14 is the city on the fire, and the death of Ezekiel's wife in 24:15–18 is the sign of the Temple's loss. The survivor who brings the news arrives in 33:21.
